The Harry Thaw Murder of Stanford White. In June 1906, wealthy rail heir Harry Thaw shot and killed renowned architect Stanford White in a public venue over the affections of actress Evelyn Nesbit, with whom both men had been involved. Thaw's subsequent trials explored insanity, moral worth, and the boundaries of American justice. Though acquitted on grounds of temporary insanity, he remained controversial, and White's death marked a high point in Gilded Age scandal and transgressive behavior.

Stanford White was a celebrated architect and co-founder of McKim, Mead and White. He was shot three times at point-blank range by Harry K. Thaw on June 25, 1906, atop Madison Square Garden's roof garden in New York. Harry Thaw was a wealthy railroad heir and known wastrel, who had married Evelyn Nesbit, a young actress and model, in 1905. She had previously been intimate with White.

Thaw was consumed with jealous rage, believing White had ruined Nesbit before their marriage. He had obsessed over Nesbit's prior relationship with the prominent architect for months. The trial came in 1907 and was sensational. Nesbit testified about her intimate history with White. Psychiatric experts debated whether Thaw was sane or temporarily insane at the moment of killing.

Thaw's defense successfully argued temporary insanity, an inability to control impulse, a novel legal strategy at the time, and he was acquitted in April 1907. This verdict troubled many who believed him guilty but simply privileged by his wealth. Thaw was committed to an asylum, then released and re-committed multiple times over subsequent decades, complicating the case's legal closure and raising questions about justice and wealth.

The case epitomized Gilded Age sexual scandal, architectural patronage, and the power of wealth to evade full accountability for crime.
